method: 5100 tonnes sand boron lead dolomite clay dropped by 1800+ helicopter sorties (Mi-26 Mi-8); sand to smother fire; lead for radiation shielding (partially counterproductive at high temp); boron carbide for neutron absorption; nitrogen injection final extinguishment
effectiveness: Fire extinguished May 9-10; releases reduced but not eliminated until full extinguishment; sand/dolomite more effective than lead drops; boron neutron absorption largely irrelevant (fission already ended)
doses_to_workers: Helicopter pilots: 1-30 mSv per sortie; some received several hundred mSv over multiple sorties; 3 pilots killed in helicopter crash April 26 (not from radiation); see unscear_liquidator_doses_REAL.csv
cost_or_resources: 5100 tonnes materials; 1800+ sorties; Mi-26 helicopters at €100k+ operating cost per sortie (approximate)

method: Remote robots attempted first (Joker; STR-1; Mobot-ChHV; German Joule robots): all failed in high radiation field (electronics destroyed); Human 'biorobots' used: workers given 1-3 minutes each to shovel graphite/fuel fragments off roof; doses 0.1-0.3 Gy per 1-3 minute shift
effectiveness: Roof decontaminated by October 1986; graphite and fuel fragments removed; dose rates on Unit 3 roof reduced from >30 Sv/hr to ~0.1-1 Sv/hr
doses_to_workers: Workers received 100-300 mGy in single 1-3 minute shift; total dose to all roof workers: 80,000 man-mGy estimated; heaviest doses of any cleanup task
cost_or_resources: ~3700 workers on roof cleanup phase; remote robot procurement costs unknown; total ~€50M equivalent in 1986 prices (rough)

method: Top 5-15 cm of soil removed by scrapers and bulldozers; soil loaded into dump trucks; taken to 800+ burial sites within CEZ; some sites properly lined; most not lined; removed soil volume: estimated 2.5 million m³; decontaminated area surface: ~500 km² priority areas
effectiveness: Reduced ambient dose rates by factor 3-10x in treated areas immediately; however in Red Forest and highest-contamination areas, soil removal was impractical; buried waste now leaches Sr-90 to groundwater; see red_forest_waste_sites_REAL.csv
doses_to_workers: Workers: 3-50 mGy per shift typical; cumulative doses for soil workers: 50-300 mGy over months
cost_or_resources: ~2.5 million m³ soil; 800+ burial sites; equipment (scrapers bulldozers dump trucks) decontaminated or buried after use; see chernobyl_economic_impact_REAL.csv for total costs

method: High-pressure washing; scrubbing of building exteriors; removal of contaminated furniture/materials from buildings; replacement of topsoil in yards; contaminated water collected and deposited; Prypiat buildings decontaminated but residents never returned; some other 30km zone villages partially decontaminated
effectiveness: Prypiat dose rates reduced from 1-10 mSv/h (1986) to 0.1-0.5 mSv/h (post-decontamination); long-term: dose rates crept back up as outdoor soil recontaminated buildings via resuspension and rain; current Prypiat ~5 µSv/h (decontamination effect eroded over 40 years)
doses_to_workers: Building wash workers: 10-100 mGy typical over multi-week assignments
cost_or_resources: ~30,000 buildings cleaned; high-pressure water systems; chemical decontaminants; costs part of $12.6B Soviet 1986-1989 total expenditure

method: Road paving; soil removal; building cleaning; city retained as administrative center for exclusion zone; dose rates reduced to allow daytime worker occupation; ~13000 original residents never returned
effectiveness: Chernobyl city dose rates: 1986 ~2-5 µSv/h immediately post-accident (lower than Prypiat due to greater distance); after decontamination ~0.1-0.5 µSv/h; current (2026): 0.209 µSv/h (SaveEcoBot)
doses_to_workers: Lower doses than Prypiat cleanup; city maintained for worker accommodation
cost_or_resources: Part of overall exclusion zone management costs; Chernobyl city serves as administration/infrastructure hub

method: Sand filter beds installed at Kyiv water intake to intercept Cs-137 on suspended particles; underground water intake from Desna River (alternative to Dnieper) developed; WHO technical assistance on removing radionuclides from water treatment
effectiveness: Cs-137 removal: >95% by coagulation-sedimentation-filtration; Sr-90 removal: 20-50% (dissolved = harder to remove); Kyiv tap water remained below WHO limits throughout crisis despite elevated raw water; see dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv
doses_to_workers: Water plant workers: minimal doses; treated as routine occupational exposure
cost_or_resources: Emergency filter installation: rapid; permanent upgrade to Kyiv water treatment; costs included in Ukrainian government Chernobyl expenditure

method: Protective earthen berm (~7m high) built around cooling pond to prevent Sr-90 contaminated water escaping to Prypiat River and Dnieper during flooding; sheet piling installed along riverbank; groundwater pumping to intercept contaminated plume from NPP
effectiveness: Partially effective: berm prevented major surface water escape during normal conditions; however flood events 1988 and 1991 still showed elevated Sr-90 in Pripyat River (see dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv); 2014 cooling pond drawdown bypassed berm effectiveness
doses_to_workers: Construction workers: 10-50 mGy over berm construction period
cost_or_resources: Earthmoving equipment; sheet piling; long-term groundwater pump operation costs; maintenance required indefinitely
source: dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv; Bugai 2022 Sci Rep; IAEA Environmental Consequences 2003

method: K fertilizer application (reduces Cs-137 plant uptake 33-50%); liming (reduces Sr-90 uptake by raising soil pH and Ca²⁺ competition); crop restriction zones; supply of uncontaminated food to contaminated areas; livestock screening before slaughter; prohibition of milk use from certain areas; annual monitoring
effectiveness: K fertilizer + liming: most cost-effective long-term intervention; reduces Cs-137 in grain 30-70% and Sr-90 30-50%; must be applied annually; by 2000: significant fraction of contaminated farmland returned to use with these measures; grain Sr-90 exceedances still occurring 2011-2019 near CEZ perimeter (ukraine_crop_contamination_REAL.csv)
doses_to_workers: Farmers: occupational exposure from working contaminated soil; typically <10 mSv/yr after initial years
cost_or_resources: Belarus spent 22.3% national budget 1991 on Chernobyl (includes agricultural support); annual K fertilizer and liming programs ongoing; see chernobyl_economic_impact_REAL.csv

method: Hexacyanoferrate (Prussian Blue analog) 'boli' (slow-release capsules) given to cattle and sheep; boli slowly dissolve in rumen; Fe-Fe(CN)6 binds Cs-137 in rumen; prevents Cs-137 absorption into blood; reduces milk/meat Cs-137 by 70-90%; proven countermeasure for farms in contaminated areas UK, Scandinavia, Russia
effectiveness: Very effective: milk Cs-137 reduced by factor 3-10 in treated cattle; widely used in UK Cumbria/Wales farms after 1986; UK adopted as standard for farms above limit; Prussian Blue oral given to humans to reduce Cs-137 after internal contamination (also used for Cs-137 ARS treatment at Goiania Brazil 1987)
doses_to_workers: None: Prussian Blue is pharmacologically inert; approved as drug for cesium poisoning
cost_or_resources: Low cost: few dollars per boli; logistically simple; most cost-effective single countermeasure per mSv dose avoided

method: 800+ radioactive waste burial and temporary storage sites created 1986-1991: include soil burial pits; building debris dumps; contaminated equipment graveyards; vehicle graveyards (1600+ vehicles at Rossokha site); some sites with partial containment; most unlined; ongoing monitoring; plans for consolidation in permanent repository
effectiveness: Partial containment: most sites are unlined pits; Sr-90 leaches to groundwater; contamination migrating downgradient; 'zombie' contamination pathway persists indefinitely; formal radioactive waste repositories not yet built (required by 2064 decommission plan)
doses_to_workers: Workers involved in waste site construction: high doses 1986-1987; current monitoring workers: low doses with PPE
cost_or_resources: ~2.5 million m³ waste volume; no formal cost estimate for permanent repository (not yet built); interim monitoring ~$5M/year

effectiveness: 1600+ vehicles (helicopters; military trucks; fire engines; buses; armored vehicles) used in cleanup and contaminated by fallout; brought to Rossokha near Burakivka for storage; dose rates on vehicles 100+ µSv/h; became informal tourist site until 2007 when vehicles were scrapped (steel sold as scrap, though some metal smelters refused contaminated steel); some vehicles still present
doses_to_workers: Vehicles represent mobile secondary contamination sources if metal is recycled; Cs-137 and Sr-90 in vehicle materials; metal recycling would disperse contamination; scrapping in 2007 was controversial but necessary for safety
cost_or_resources: Workers scrapping/managing vehicles: 0.5-5 µSv/h on site
source: Vehicle scrapping 2007; disposal costs unknown; represents permanent removal of ~2000 tonnes contaminated steel
column9: modern_monitoring_REAL.csv; IAEA Environmental Consequences; multiple photojournalism sources

method: Plants (Helianthus annuus sunflower; Brassica juncea Indian mustard) tested for phytoremediation: sunflower roots float on contaminated water and concentrate Cs-137 from water (bioconcentration factor 10000-30000 from solution); Indian mustard concentrates Sr-90; after harvest plants incinerate to small ash volume; demonstrated in Chernobyl cooling pond 1996
effectiveness: Effective for contaminated water (swimming pools; ponds); less effective for soil because bioavailability of soil Cs-137 declines with aging (fixation); Chernobyl cooling pond trial showed 5-10 Bq/L reduction in surface water Cs-137 with floating sunflowers; not scaled for full CEZ remediation due to cost and biomass management
doses_to_workers: Workers growing and harvesting plants: minimal exposure with gloves
cost_or_resources: Research-scale; demonstration cost ~$1-5M; not cost-effective for full-scale CEZ decontamination
source: Dushenkov V 1997 Environ Sci Technol PMID:21654075; Duke 2001; IAEA Phytoremediation; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv

method: Dead pine trees cut down and buried in unlined trenches (500-1000 cubic meters per trench; ~2-3m deep; 30-50 meters long); sawdust and chips added; plastic sheeting attempted but inadequate; site covered with approximately 50 cm clean soil cap
effectiveness: FAILED to contain Sr-90: trench burial created pathway for Sr-90 leaching to groundwater; groundwater Sr-90 in Red Forest trenches 3-4 orders magnitude above WHO guideline; the burial WORSENED the groundwater contamination by concentrating fuel particles and creating preferential flow paths
doses_to_workers: Workers who buried Red Forest trees: among highest doses of any cleanup workers; not well-documented retrospectively
cost_or_resources: Burial itself cost: excavation equipment + ~6 weeks of work for teams; long-term: ongoing Sr-90 contamination monitoring and groundwater treatment costs
